newsitem.title: USA: MCI cuts in-state toll rates in 40 states.
newsitem.headline: MCI cuts in-state toll rates in 40 states.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp said Monday it plans to shake up the $6 billion residential local toll call market with a nationwide plan that offers flat-rate pricing at substantial discounts to those of rival Baby Bells.

MCI, the second largest U.S. long-distance provider, said its new flat rate local toll call plan will provide consumers savings in all fifty states, with the rates depending on pricing structures set by regulators within each state.
The price cuts vary, but in 40 of the states, consumers would save from 15 to 59 percent versus regional Bell companies' average basic rates for local toll calls, MCI said.
In the remaining ten states, the plan would result in single-digit savings, an MCI spokeswoman said.
Local toll calls are calls placed within a specific geographic region, yet outside the local calling area.
As an example, MCI said California consumers would be charged at a flat rate of $0.04 a minute under its plan, or 42 percent less than Pacific Bell's average basic rates.
Pacific Bell is the dominant supplier of local phone services, including toll calls in Northern California and Nevada. It was recently acquired by San Antonio-based SBC Communications Inc.
According to MCI calculations, a five-minute evening call from San Jose to San Francisco costs $0.52 using Pacific Bell versus $0.20 for an MCI customer.
In Texas, MCI consumers will pay a rate of $0.12 a minute, 44 percent below the average basic rates of SBC, the dominant local carrier in five central and southwestern states.
A five-minute evening call from Houston to Galveston would cost $0.60 using MCI versus $1.35 via SBC.
All new and current MCI customers are eligible to sign up for the new flat rate plan and existing MCI One customers will automatically receive the new rates, the company said.
"MCI's local toll pricing is a clear example of how consumers will benefit from competition," Judy Levine, MCI's executive director of brand marketing, said in a statement.
Local toll calls typically are itemized on phone bills as local or regional toll calls and in some states can be more expensive than long-distance calls, despite a shorter geographic distance.

Historically, all local toll calls were handled by local telephone carriers, which prior to reforms introduced as part of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 operated as virtual monopolies within their respective geographic regions.

Gradually, other companies, such as MCI, have been authorized to compete for local toll service. This means consumers can pick a company to handle their local toll calls -- much like they do today with long-distance companies.
An MCI spokeswoman said the company will introduce a television and radio marketing campaign in California Monday evening trumpeting the lower local calling rates.
In November, MCI agreed to merge with British Telecommunications Plc in a deal valued at more than $20 billion. The deal awaits U.S. regulatory approvals.
